subject: botany
question_text: Describe the non-essential floral parts of plants belonging to Fabaceae.

verification.note: Chapter 8 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack botany section (book pp.21-22), which prints the question and a model answer but NO star rank and NO year citation — so `stars` is 0 and `appearances` is empty by construction, not by omission. Only ONE botany source book is held: there is no TSBIE Basic Learning Material for botany (the copy in hand is physics-only) and no botany board paper in the corpus, so the two-book union check and the back-test against a real paper are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this chapter. steps.label: Calyx
lines: Five sepals, gamosepalous (fused into a tube).
steps.why: Non-essential means the whorls that do not take part in reproduction, so the answer is the calyx and the corolla only.
common_mistakes: Describing the stamens. Those are essential parts and earn nothing here.
Writing polysepalous. Fabaceae sepals are fused.
steps.memory_tip: Non-essential = the two outer whorls. Essential = the two inner whorls.
steps.margin_note: Head the block "Calyx" and give three short facts.

steps.label: Corolla
lines: Five petals, polypetalous, and papilionaceous in
two anterior keel petals (carina) fused along
their lower edge, enclosing the stamens and the
steps.why: The papilionaceous corolla is the one feature that names the whole sub-family, so the three kinds of petal must be named separately.
common_mistakes: Writing five equal petals. The five petals are of three different kinds.
Writing gamopetalous. The petals are free; only the two keel petals are joined to each other.
steps.memory_tip: One standard, two wings, two keel: 1 + 2 + 2 = 5 petals.
steps.margin_note: Name all three petal types with their Latin names in brackets.

steps.label: Diagram
steps.why: The shape of the corolla is easier to show than to describe, and the examiner marks the drawing for the three named petal types in their correct positions.
common_mistakes: Putting the standard petal at the bottom. It is the posterior, uppermost petal.
steps.memory_tip: Draw it top down: the big standard first, the two wings next, the boat-shaped keel last.
steps.margin_note: A simple line drawing with the three petal types labelled earns the full diagram mark.

steps.label: Aestivation
lines: It is descendingly imbricate: the standard petal
covers the two wings, and each wing covers one
steps.why: Vexillary aestivation is named after the vexillum, and it simply records which petal overlaps which.
common_mistakes: Writing twisted aestivation. That is Malvaceae.
Naming vexillary but not saying which petal overlaps which.
steps.memory_tip: Vexillum means flag or standard. Vexillary aestivation is named after it: the standard petal covers the rest.
steps.margin_note: Name the aestivation and give the overlap order in one line.

insider_note: The corolla carries this question. If time is short, draw the papilionaceous corolla and label it before writing the calyx.
